title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
authors: Marcos Crichigno, Steve Flammia
abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents improved quantum circuit compilation through iterative program optimization, with every result certified by a frozen, exact verifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could lower quantum implementation costs while making automated optimization results independently checkable.
method: An agent formulates the optimization challenge with a researcher and builds an exact verifier.
Validate the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results, then freeze it.
Agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and record reusable insights in human-readable notes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis, agents reduced optimized costs by up to 73% at the largest tested sizes and outperformed a state-of-the-art fermion-to-qubit encoding optimizer.
infographic.watch_item: The method requires exact, efficient verification; reported cost reductions do not by themselves establish end-to-end hardware speedups.
infographic.paper_title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents

title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods
authors: Vitor Dallabona, Lucas Friedrich, Jonas Maziero
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

infographic.key_insight: QAOA and FALQON follow distinct entanglement and coherence trajectories as they approach Minimum Vertex Cover solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tracking these resource trajectories can inform circuit-depth and algorithm choices for near-term quantum optimization without requiring full state tomography.
method: Apply QAOA and FALQON to a Minimum Vertex Cover instance.
Optimize auxiliary quantum circuits to identify closest resource-free states using the Bures metric and Uhlmann’s theorem.
Track Bures entanglement and coherence as optimization progresses.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the studied instance, QAOA shows an early entanglement peak and residual coherence, while FALQON shows a lower, later peak and smoothly decreasing coherence alongside optimization error.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports one problem instance, so generalization to larger graphs and noisy hardware remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods

title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models
authors: Tariq Mahassen, Marcin Jastrzebski, Oleksandr Kyriienko
abstract: We develop and analyze generative models based on quantum solvers of stochastic differential equations. Unlike the common approach based on layered variational quantum circuits with parameterized rotations, we parameterize the potential of a Langevin process. The associated Fokker-Planck (FP) equations are Hermitianized and solved using a linear combination of cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation. By encoding the square root of the stationary density, the model enables sampling through computational-basis measurements and is efficiently controlled by coefficients of the block-encoded diagonal potential. We train the proposed model to match empirical distributions within the family described by FP equations, demonstrating parameter recovery for multivariate probability distributions. Crucially, the model remains trainable at scale. Sample-efficient and convex optimization for in-distribution targets arises from a physics-informed inductive bias and holds regardless of the dimensionality of the problem. We provide circuit constructions and efficient block encodings of the main components of the algorithm and analyze resource requirements. Our approach frames quantum generative learning as quantum model discovery and provides a foundation for extending this framework to high-dimensional, strongly correlated scientific data.

infographic.key_insight: Trainable quantum generative models can learn a Langevin potential rather than circuit rotations, using quantum Fokker–Planck solvers to prepare and sample probability distributions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-informed parameterization offers a route to scalable quantum generative learning for scientific distributions governed by stochastic dynamics.
method: Parameterize the Langevin potential and Hermitianize its Fokker–Planck equation.
Solve using a linear combination of cosine operators implemented through quantum singular value transformation.
Encode the stationary density’s square root and sample via computational-basis measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parameter recovery for multivariate distributions and sample-efficient, convex optimization for in-distribution targets, with circuit constructions and resource analysis.
infographic.watch_item: The trainability guarantees concern in-distribution targets; practical feasibility also depends on efficient block encoding and quantum circuit resources.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Fokker-Planck solvers as trainable generative models

title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry
authors: G. X. A. Petronilo, M. R. Araújo, Erico S. Teixeira, Clebson Cruz
abstract: Predicting molecular electronic structure using Quantum Computing approaches is a challenge in Computational Chemistry. Traditional Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically hindered by optimization challenges. The alternative Generative Quantum Eigensolver (GQE) mitigates this by reformulating ground-state search as discrete sequence generation, but its Transformer backbone suffers from quadratic computational complexity, bottlenecking scalability for larger molecules. To address this, we introduce the Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (Mamba-QE), which replaces the Transformer with a Selective State Space Model (SSM) to process operator sequences with linear $\mathcal{O}(L)$ complexity. Additionally, we integrate a distance-conditioned mechanism enabling the direct prediction of complete potential energy surfaces (PES). Evaluated on the $H_2$ molecule, Mamba-QE reproduces Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) reference energies well within chemical accuracy, achieving an energy error below $3\times10^{-6}$ Ha across 16 geometries with zero variational violations. Mamba-QE maintains high expressive power while establishing a robust, scalable foundation for quantum simulations of complex molecular systems.

infographic.key_insight: Mamba-QE replaces the Transformer in a generative quantum eigensolver with a selective state space model, enabling linear-complexity operator-sequence processing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture addresses sequence-processing costs in molecular ground-state simulation, though scalability beyond H₂ remains unverified in the abstract.
method: Reformulate ground-state search as discrete quantum-operator sequence generation.
Use a Mamba selective state space model with O(L) sequence-processing complexity.
Condition generation on interatomic distance to predict potential energy surfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: On H₂ across 16 geometries, the abstract reports energy errors below 3×10⁻⁶ Ha relative to Full Configuration Interaction, with zero variational violations.
infographic.watch_item: Linear sequence-processing complexity does not establish end-to-end simulation scalability; larger-molecule validation is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Mamba Quantum Eigensolver (MQE): A Selective State Space Model for Scalable Ground State Simulations in Quantum Chemistry

title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields
authors: Zhiyao Li
abstract: Matter under extreme conditions behaves as a non-equilibrium, strongly-interacting quantum system. Such systems are in the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), where their time evolution is classically intractable. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative, but present-day devices are limited in qubit count and circuit depth, so efficient formulations and algorithms are key to scaling toward experimentally relevant QCD simulations. A scalable framework is established for simulating energy loss and hadronization in 1+1-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory, in which a heavy quark traverses a lattice of light quarks. Classical lattice QCD methods are translated into physics-informed circuits to prepare the interacting ground state. The evolution is run on IBM's quantum processor ibm_pittsburgh, where the charge distribution and energy loss are measured. A further study develops the quantum simulation of the fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis, a formulation that is expected to remain efficient at all gauge couplings. Digitizing the continuous gauge fields with as few as three qubits per plaquette reproduces low-energy observables with $10^{-3}$ precision. Scaling to larger systems is limited by resource overhead, which motivates truncations that preserve the relevant observables. Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) exploits the hierarchy in basis-operator contributions. Demonstrated on the adiabatic preparation of the $λφ^4$ ground state on ibm_sherbrooke, SeqHT reduces circuit depth by ~30%, suppressing hardware noise in the extracted observables. All simulations in this dissertation are validated on quantum hardware against classical benchmarks. These studies advance quantum simulations of real-time QCD dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed circuits, compact gauge-field digitization, and operator truncation advance hardware demonstrations toward real-time simulations of strongly interacting quantum fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These techniques reduce qubit and circuit-depth requirements for lattice-field simulations relevant to QCD dynamics.
method: Prepare interacting ground states and simulate a heavy quark traversing light quarks in 1+1D SU(2) lattice gauge theory.
Digitize a fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis using as few as three qubits per plaquette.
Apply Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) during adiabatic preparation of a λφ⁴ ground state.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports hardware validation against classical benchmarks, low-energy observables reproduced to 10⁻³ precision with compact digitization, and about 30% circuit-depth reduction from SeqHT.
infographic.watch_item: Resource overhead still limits larger systems, and truncations must preserve the observables of interest.
infographic.paper_title: Digital Quantum Simulation of Dynamics in Interacting Fields

title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations
authors: Giuseppe Bisicchia, Alessandro Bocci, Jose Garcia-Alonso, Juan Manuel Murillo, Antonio Brogi
abstract: Cloud-accessible quantum computing has made heterogeneous Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) available through provider platforms that differ in qubit technology, calibration state, queueing behavior, and pricing model. This heterogeneity makes execution management a quantum-engineering concern: a quantum circuit may be executable on several backends, but the resulting cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility depend on backend selection and on how measurement shots are allocated. This paper presents the Quantum Broker, an open-source and provider-agnostic framework for Quality-of-Service-aware quantum execution management. The framework operationalizes shot-wise distribution by exploiting the statistical independence of quantum measurement shots to dispatch a single circuit across multiple heterogeneous QPUs according to user-defined constraints and optimization objectives. It combines a modular execution architecture, interchangeable backend-profiling strategies, and the Quantum QoS Specification Language (QQSpec), a declarative language for expressing QoS requirements. Dispatch planning is supported by two solver backends: a mixed-integer linear-programming (MILP) solver, and a nonlinear dual-annealing solver. Experiments on benchmark quantum circuits and noisy simulator backends show that the Quantum Broker can produce feasible QoS-aware dispatch plans under heterogeneous backend conditions and can improve QoS satisfaction with respect to single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines. The results also expose a practical trade-off between planning time and dispatch quality, with the nonlinear solver producing higher-quality allocations at increased computational cost. Overall, the Quantum Broker provides an extensible execution-management layer for engineering portable, reproducible, and QoS-aware quantum software over fragmented quantum cloud infrastructures.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Broker distributes a circuit’s measurement shots across heterogeneous QPUs to meet user-defined quality-of-service constraints and objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its provider-agnostic execution layer helps engineers manage cost, latency, fidelity, and reproducibility across fragmented quantum cloud platforms.
method: Exploit statistically independent measurement shots to split execution across QPUs.
Express QoS requirements with QQSpec and characterize backends through interchangeable profiling strategies.
Optimize shot allocations using MILP or nonlinear dual-annealing solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmark-circuit experiments on noisy simulators produced feasible QoS-aware plans and improved QoS satisfaction over single-backend and naive multi-backend baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Real-hardware validation remains important; the nonlinear solver improved allocation quality but required more planning time.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Broker: QoS-Aware Distribution of Quantum Computations

title: Symmetry-Preserving and Scalable Variational Circuits for the Lattice Gross-Neveu Model
authors: Vivan Bhatt, Zhongtian Dong, Kyoungchul Kong, Kwangmin Yu
abstract: We study variational preparation of ground states and sector-resolved excited states in the $(1+1)$-dimensional lattice Gross-Neveu model. We construct fixed circuits preserving either total fermion number or every flavor number, and a problem-specific scalable-circuit adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (SC-ADAPT-VQE). Classical circuit benchmarks cover massless and massive systems through 30 qubits, using exact-diagonalization and tensor-network reference results. Imposing flavor-number conservation improves the achieved energies in the completed two-flavor comparisons. Selected massive fixed-ansatz benchmarks with one to four flavors have relative energy errors of approximately $1 \times 10^{-5}$ - $2 \times 10^{-4}$, smaller than the quoted literature errors where available, although discretizations and computational resources differ. The adaptive pool combines translated bulk and boundary-sensitive generators with an interaction-sensitive cross-flavor family. Selected massive SC-ADAPT benchmarks with one to three flavors have relative energy errors below $2.1 \times 10^{-3}$. For one flavor, matrix-product-state evaluations extend the transferred circuits to 60-400 qubits without target-side operator selection or parameter optimization, giving energy deviations of approximately $0.35\%$ - $1.76\%$ from density-matrix renormalization-group reference values at maximum bond dimension 256. At fixed flavor number, range caps, and append count, the adaptive construction has a precompilation local-factor count linear in volume and a volume-independent shared-parameter count; fixed-accuracy performance at arbitrary volumes remains unestablished. Sequential deflation also prepares low-lying states within a fixed flavor-number sector, with projector fidelities providing a basis-independent assessment of degenerate target eigenspaces.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetry-preserving variational circuits improve lattice Gross–Neveu energy estimates, while adaptive circuits enable parameter transfer to larger systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The adaptive construction offers linear precompilation local-factor growth with volume and a volume-independent shared-parameter count when flavor number, range caps, and append count are fixed.
method: Build fixed ansätze preserving total fermion number or each flavor number.
Use SC-ADAPT-VQE with bulk, boundary-sensitive, and cross-flavor generators.
Prepare sector-resolved excited states by sequential deflation and assess degenerate eigenspaces using projector fidelities.
infographic.evidence_signal: Classical benchmarks reach 30 qubits; selected massive fixed ansätze achieve relative energy errors of about 10⁻⁵–2×10⁻⁴, while one-flavor circuits transferred to 60–400 qubits show 0.35%–1.76% deviations from DMRG references without target-side optimization.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed-accuracy scaling to arbitrary volumes remains unestablished, and the reported evaluations are classical circuit and tensor-network benchmarks rather than quantum-hardware demonstrations.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetry-Preserving and Scalable Variational Circuits for the Lattice Gross-Neveu Model

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
authors: Chia-Hsien Huang, Hsi-Sheng Goan
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

infographic.key_insight: Optimized flux pulses enable 12-ns controlled-Z gates with intrinsic errors near 2×10⁻⁵, while revealing operating regimes resilient to dephasing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps superconducting quantum hardware designers balance gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness, potentially reducing recalibration overhead.
method: Optimize smooth, single-shot flux pulses for directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons.
Model intrinsic Hamiltonian errors, energy relaxation, and fast and slow dephasing.
Identify dephasing sweet spots and exploit transmon asymmetry for noise resilience.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 12-ns gates near an 11.6-ns theoretical speed limit and dephasing models calibrated against published experimental measurements.
infographic.watch_item: The reported intrinsic error excludes decoherence contributions; hardware performance requires validation under device-specific noise.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence

title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
authors: Ouns El Harzli, Jelle Bor, Linde Wester, Leonid Zhukov, Hanl Park, Jean-François Bobier
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum impurity solvers could enable more accurate screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials, but quantum advantage remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links electrode-interface energetics and conductivity to solid oxide fuel cell and electrolyser performance, then to potential business value.
method: Shortlist materials with DFT and construct correlated impurity models from electrode–electrolyte interfaces.
Use quantum impurity solvers within GW+DMFT or SEET to calculate finite-temperature Green’s functions.
Connect vacancy energetics and transport properties to continuum electrode models and deployment scenarios.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports illustrative logical-qubit counts and scenario-based value estimates, while identifying convergence tests and classical-solver comparisons needed to assess quantum advantage.
infographic.watch_item: Complete resource estimates must include thermal-state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated impurity solves—not just qubit counts.
infographic.paper_title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation

title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
authors: Joseph Sullivan, David Amaro, Michael A. Perlin
abstract: We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.

infographic.key_insight: Preparing and consuming logical resource states enables addressable, parallel universal fault-tolerant computation in high-rate concatenated quantum codes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This architecture shifts logical-gate implementation toward resource-state preparation and error-correcting teleportation, offering a route to lower fault-tolerant computing overhead.
method: Concatenate small-distance, high-rate self-dual CSS codes.
Prepare logical CSS stabilizer states with flag-at-origin and global magic states with concatenated cultivation.
Consume resources through Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation, requiring at most 12 resource states per T-depth layer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Resource-preparation benchmarks for several two-level concatenations of H codes and the [[15,7,3]] Hamming code report at least a tenfold spacetime reduction for concatenated cultivation versus surface-code cultivation.
infographic.watch_item: The reported advantage concerns resource preparation; full-system benefits require evaluating hardware connectivity, noise assumptions, and resource delivery overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes

title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation
authors: Zhengyi Liu, Li Liu, Songtao Liu, Xianglong Liu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Mingyu Huang
abstract: Tensor-network simulation of quantum circuits depends on contraction orders with low computational cost and small intermediate tensors, found without excessive planning time. We present ArcTN, a contraction-order optimization framework with two search presets. Light keeps planning overhead low, and Heavy spends more effort on refinement. Both combine randomized-greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering with stage-specific stopping rules. ArcTN also provides Fixed and Dynamic slicing to meet tensor-size limits and executes the returned orders. On the 30 QC32 quantum-circuit networks completed by all eight compared configurations, Light reduces FLOPs by 61.32% and plans 1.62$\times$ faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA-ES, and Heavy reduces FLOPs by 43.83% and plans 7.21$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ/Optuna. Heavy also needs 11.85% fewer FLOPs than OMECO TreeSA-8 and plans 1.33$\times$ faster. Dynamic slicing meets the size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar-output networks and reduces total sliced FLOPs by 31.99% relative to Fixed slicing, at the cost of longer planning. With a common NumPy executor, Heavy has the lowest combined planning and execution time among five configurations on the runs that all of them completed. On 672 networks built from 320 MQT Bench circuits, Heavy obtains the lowest geometric-mean FLOPs on the 142 large networks while planning 3.1$\times$ and 31$\times$ faster than Cotengra AutoHQ and Hyper128.

infographic.key_insight: ArcTN finds lower-cost tensor-network contraction orders while reducing planning time, improving the efficiency of quantum circuit simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Light and Heavy search presets balance planning effort against contraction cost, while slicing helps keep intermediate tensors within size limits.
method: Combine randomized-greedy construction, subtree reconfiguration, and parallel tempering.
Use stage-specific stopping rules with Light and Heavy search presets.
Apply Fixed or Dynamic slicing to meet tensor-size limits, then execute the returned orders.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 30 QC32 networks completed by all eight configurations, Light used 61.32% fewer FLOPs and planned 1.62× faster than Cotengra Auto/CMA-ES; Dynamic slicing met size limits in all 90 runs on 18 scalar-output networks.
infographic.watch_item: Dynamic slicing requires longer planning, and several reported performance comparisons include only runs completed by all compared configurations.
infographic.paper_title: ArcTN: Efficient Tensor-Network Contraction Planning for Quantum Circuit Simulation

title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
authors: Brian Coyle, Jonathan H. Fetherolf, Antonio Márquez Romero, Stefano Scali, Giuseppe Buonaiuto, Josh Kirsopp
abstract: Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.

infographic.key_insight: StateDRIFT tailors randomised Hamiltonian sampling to the initial state and target observable, reducing estimation bias and variance while retaining qDRIFT’s guarantees through a provable truncation bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Problem-aware sampling can reduce circuit depth and two-qubit gate requirements for estimating quantum dynamics at a target accuracy.
method: Optimise term-sampling probabilities at each depth to target bias and/or variance.
Use initial-state observables and commutators to inform the optimisation.
Estimate required quantities with classical surrogates, such as tensor networks, or classical shadows.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on short-time lattice and molecular dynamics up to 18 qubits included a BeH2 example reducing two-qubit gates from 11,201 to 983 at a given accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Practical savings depend on the cost and accuracy of estimating the state-dependent quantities needed for sampling optimisation.
infographic.paper_title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation

title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis
authors: Bikalpa Gautam, Akil Raj Subedi
abstract: Amplitude encoding stores an N-degree-of-freedom structural mode using ceiling(log2 N) qubits. This article develops an evaluation framework for variational quantum eigensolvers in finite-element structural dynamics. A Cholesky transformation maps the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric mass-orthonormal Hamiltonian, ensuring Euclidean quantum-state orthogonality equals structural mass orthogonality. For higher modes, the deflation penalty condition is sharpened to a necessary-and-sufficient threshold, with a Davis-Kahan bound quantifying effects of approximate projectors. Numerical studies separate mapping correctness, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, finite-shot uncertainty, and damage localization. For 128-DOF chains, consistent-mass whitening increases transformed-operator density from 0.023 to 0.308 and Pauli terms from 576 to 2950. Exact state-vector experiments show qubit count and circuit expressibility are distinct. At 10^5 shots per Pauli term, first-mode frequency RMS error is 2.45%. In an oracle-state study, 10% stiffness loss is localized in 84.5% of trials. Results sharpen the deflation condition, quantify resource bottlenecks, and claim no speedup.

infographic.key_insight: Logarithmic qubit encoding is not enough for practical quantum modal analysis: deflation accuracy, circuit expressibility, and measurement costs remain critical.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework evaluates variational quantum eigensolvers for structural vibration modes and damage localization while preserving mass orthogonality.
method: Use Cholesky whitening to map the generalized eigenproblem to a symmetric Hamiltonian.
Derive a necessary-and-sufficient deflation threshold and bound approximate-projector errors.
Evaluate mapping, ansatz expressibility, preprocessing, Pauli growth, and finite-shot uncertainty separately.
infographic.evidence_signal: For 128-DOF chains, whitening increased Pauli terms from 576 to 2,950; first-mode frequency RMS error was 2.45% at 100,000 shots per term, and an oracle-state study localized 10% stiffness loss in 84.5% of trials.
infographic.watch_item: Dense transformed operators and costly measurements can offset compact encoding; oracle-state localization does not establish end-to-end hardware performance, and no speedup is claimed.
infographic.paper_title: Qubits Are Not Enough: Deflation and Measurement Limits in Variational Quantum Modal Analysis

title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
authors: Md Khalid Syfullah, Alvi Ataur Khalil
abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

infographic.key_insight: Simulated quantum layers can improve vision-language accuracy or reduce trainable parameters, but benefits depend strongly on placement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Selective quantum-layer integration offers a design path for hybrid VLMs, though parameter savings do not reliably reduce training time or computation.
method: Use LLaVA-OneVision with classically simulated 4- and 8-qubit circuits.
Test basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations.
Compare accuracy and computational cost, and evaluate robustness under six attack settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Visual Spatial Reasoning development data, post-projector insertion reaches 80.7% accuracy (+2.28 percentage points over classical full fine-tuning), while final decoder feed-forward replacement retains 79.22% with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters.
infographic.watch_item: These simulation-based results do not establish quantum-hardware speedups, generalizable gains, or a security advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?

title: Normal-Form Characterization of Adaptivity and Entanglement in Pauli-Based Computation
authors: Filipa C. R. Peres, Selman Ipek, Daniel Lovsted, Joshua Nevin, Anne Broadbent
abstract: Pauli-based computation (PBC) is a measurement-based model of quantum computation that samples from output distributions of universal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Here, we provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes its adaptive and entanglement structures. These insights unify PBC with one-way quantum computing as dual or `time-reversed' counterparts. We use the NF to advance strategies for distributed computation and investigate magic-state injection rates. We also demonstrate an exponential improvement in the detection of unnecessary magic-state qubits, allowing their efficient removal. Our NF further enables ahead-of-time circuit compilation using PBC, reducing CNOT gate count and quantum memory of random quantum circuits on average by 50% and 40%, respectively, beating other state-of-the-art compilers.

infographic.key_insight: A normal form for Pauli-based computation fully characterizes its adaptivity and entanglement, connecting it to one-way quantum computing as a time-reversed counterpart.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports distributed quantum computation and ahead-of-time compilation that can reduce entangling-gate overhead and quantum memory requirements.
method: Derive a normal form for Pauli-based computation.
Use its structure to analyze distributed computation and magic-state injection rates.
Efficiently identify unnecessary magic-state qubits and compile circuits ahead of execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an exponential improvement in detecting unnecessary magic-state qubits and average reductions of 50% in CNOT count and 40% in quantum memory on random quantum circuits, outperforming compared state-of-the-art compilers.
infographic.watch_item: Reported gains are averages on random circuits; benefits for practical workloads and hardware-specific constraints remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Normal-Form Characterization of Adaptivity and Entanglement in Pauli-Based Computation

title: Scalable Neural Wave Functions via Information Mixing and Hierarchical Network Architectures
authors: Faith Oyedemi, Stefanie Czischek
abstract: Numerically simulating quantum many-body systems is one of the central challenges in modern physics, as the exponential growth of the Hilbert space with system size renders large-scale exact solutions intractable. Over the past decade, generative artificial neural networks have emerged as powerful wave function ansätze that have powered advances in finding ground state representations, reconstructing quantum states from data, and modeling dynamics in quantum many-body systems. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are computationally efficient, the recurrent nature can limit their capacity to capture long-range correlations. Transformer models with their underlying self-attention mechanism excel at capturing these long-range correlations, but incur increased computational requirements, restricting applications to small physical systems. In this work, we address these limitations by exploring the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mixer model as a wave function ansatz. By mixing information globally and locally through the system via a computationally lightweight mixing strategy, this architecture promises to combine the ability to capture long-range correlations with low computational costs. We benchmark the model on finding ground state representations of two-dimensional quantum many-body systems in various phases of matter and investigate the behavior of representational accuracy and computational efficiency for different physical system sizes. By comparing its performance to RNNs and transformer models with single-site and patched input definitions, we demonstrate that the MLP mixer architecture performs competitively with state-of-the-art network models. We further show that a hierarchical combination of this model with the transformer model outperforms other state-of-the-art architectures for large-scale quantum systems, opening new avenues for investigating quantum phases of matter.

infographic.key_insight: MLP-mixer neural wave functions offer competitive quantum-state modeling, while a hierarchical mixer–transformer architecture outperforms other tested models on large quantum systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lightweight information mixing offers a route to scalable classical simulation of quantum many-body systems while balancing correlation modeling and computational cost.
method: Use an MLP mixer as a wave function ansatz to mix information globally and locally.
Benchmark against RNNs and transformers with single-site and patched inputs.
Combine the mixer and transformer in a hierarchical architecture.
infographic.evidence_signal: Ground-state benchmarks on two-dimensional quantum many-body systems across phases and sizes assess representational accuracy and computational efficiency.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical speedups, error values, or resource requirements, limiting assessment of practical scaling gains.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Neural Wave Functions via Information Mixing and Hierarchical Network Architectures

title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits
authors: Grzegorz Czelusta, Marcin Markiewicz, Jakub Mielczarek, Artur Miroszewski
abstract: Photonic and qubit-based (digital) approaches to quantum computing are largely regarded as separate paradigms. This article aims to bridge these paradigms by developing a method for mapping quantum-optical systems onto qubit-based quantum circuits. The key ingredient enabling this mapping is the introduction of a truncation of the Fock space describing single-mode optical states. Within this framework, representations of basic photonic operations are developed, including the phase-rotation operator, the displacement operator, the squeezing operator, and the beam splitter. Explicit quantum circuit constructions are provided for Fock-space truncations of dimension $N=2$ and $N=4$. We discuss benchmarking of the implemented operations and identify the regime of applicability and the limitations of the proposed method. The presented results can be used to simulate quantum optical circuits on qubit-based quantum computers, with special relevance to Gaussian Boson Sampling in the low-photon-number regime. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we complement the theoretical framework with a Python-based quantum programming tool CO$Φ$ that compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits using a truncated Fock-space encoding. The compiler is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Quantum-Cosmos-Lab/cophi.

infographic.key_insight: COΦ maps photonic quantum operations onto digital qubit circuits by encoding optical states in a truncated Fock space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its Python compiler translates Blackbird quantum-optics programs into OpenQASM circuits, enabling low-photon-number photonic simulations on qubit-based quantum computers.
method: Truncate each optical mode’s Fock space to a finite-dimensional encoding.
Construct qubit representations of phase rotation, displacement, squeezing, and beam-splitter operations.
Provide explicit circuits for truncation dimensions N=2 and N=4.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports explicit circuit constructions and discusses benchmarking, but provides no numerical accuracy or hardware-performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Fock-space truncation limits fidelity when appreciable photon-number probability lies beyond the cutoff, so applicability depends on the optical state and operations.
infographic.paper_title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits

title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm
authors: Ming Zhong, Xiangyu Ren, Kangyu Zheng, Zhi Zeng, Shenggen Zheng, Shaohua Li
abstract: Selecting an effective quantum compiler configuration requires coordinated decisions over both hardware targets and compiler settings, with the ultimate goal of improving circuit execution fidelity. Existing SOTA approaches typically decompose this problem into two sequential stages: a device is chosen first, after which compiler options are tuned on that device through RL-based search. This bottom-up strategy can be fundamentally limited by its initial device decision, since a poorly matched backend may constrain the best fidelity achievable regardless of how effectively later compiler options are optimized. In contrast to classical compiler tuning, where the search space is often prohibitively large, the configuration space of quantum compilers remains manageable enough to support exhaustive search. Consequently, rather than repeatedly searching from candidate configurations, one can derive reusable configuration knowledge from offline oracle results and apply it directly to new circuits. In this paper, we introduce a top-down configuration-selection paradigm and build QuOPTBench, an exhaustively searched benchmark containing oracle configurations for 268 quantum circuits. We first study whether LLMs can directly infer suitable configurations and evaluate ten representative LLMs. The results reveal that vanilla LLMs remain far from the oracle. We then employ an LLM to extract transferable rules from sampled circuits governing configuration selection. Using these rules together with predictors trained on the enumerated configuration data of the sampled circuits, we design QuTOP, a rule-guided ML framework that performs fast configuration selection without iterative online search. Across our evaluation, the distilled rules consistently strengthen LLM-based selection, while QuTOP provides the strongest overall balance between solution quality and selection latency among the baselines.

infographic.key_insight: QuTOP uses offline oracle configurations to guide joint hardware and compiler-setting selection, avoiding the limitations of choosing a device first.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets higher circuit execution fidelity with low selection latency and no iterative online configuration search.
method: Build QuOPTBench by exhaustively searching configurations for 268 quantum circuits.
Use an LLM to extract transferable configuration-selection rules from sampled circuits.
Combine these rules with predictors trained on enumerated configuration data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation of ten representative LLMs found vanilla models far from the oracle, while QuTOP achieved the strongest overall quality–latency balance among evaluated baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to unseen circuit families or changing hardware calibration requires validation, and offline exhaustive search adds preparation cost.
infographic.paper_title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm

title: Bias-Preserving Entanglement of Kerr-Cat Qubits with an ATS Coupler
authors: Kerem Yurtseven, Shantanu R. Jha, Apoorva Limaye, Risav Pokhrel, Muhammad Waqar Amin
abstract: Kerr-cat qubits offer a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing by suppressing bit-flip errors exponentially, while phase-flip errors increase only linearly with the mean photon number. To maintain this protection, entangling operations must be bias-preserving, ensuring that phase-flip errors occurring during the gate do not propagate into bit-flip errors. In this paper, we propose an asymmetrically threaded SQUID (ATS) parametric coupler to implement high-fidelity, bias-preserving entangling gates between Kerr-cat qubits. By engineering a photon-number asymmetry between the control and target modes, we enable fast gate operations that suppress non-adiabatic leakage without complex pulse shaping. Through numerical simulations of the full circuit Hamiltonian, we demonstrate a bias-preserving CX gate achieving 99.69% fidelity in the absence of photon loss for a gate duration of 50 ns. Under a single-photon loss rate of 100 kHz, our protocol yields a noise bias of 9922, exceeding the noise bias of a naive non-bias-preserving CX implementation by approximately a factor of 570. These results support the ATS coupler as a valuable building block for concatenated cat-qubit architectures.

infographic.key_insight: An asymmetrically threaded SQUID (ATS) coupler enables fast entangling gates that preserve Kerr-cat qubits’ protection against bit-flip errors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The proposed coupler could support concatenated cat-qubit architectures by enabling entanglement without sacrificing the noise bias needed for efficient error correction.
method: Use an ATS parametric coupler to entangle Kerr-cat qubits.
Engineer unequal photon numbers in control and target modes to suppress non-adiabatic leakage without complex pulse shaping.
Evaluate the bias-preserving CX gate through full-circuit Hamiltonian simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations report 99.69% CX fidelity in 50 ns without photon loss and a noise bias of 9922 at a 100 kHz single-photon loss rate, approximately 570 times the naive non-bias-preserving CX baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The results are numerical; experimental performance remains to be established under realistic device imperfections and additional noise channels.
infographic.paper_title: Bias-Preserving Entanglement of Kerr-Cat Qubits with an ATS Coupler

title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
authors: Andrew J. Ochoa, Martin J. A. Schuetz, Helmut G. Katzgraber
abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.

infographic.key_insight: Classical Houdayer cluster updates amplify the diversity of quantum-generated maximum independent set solutions, with gains of up to 11,923×.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Post-processing can extract more distinct high-quality configurations from existing quantum measurements without additional quantum sampling.
method: Seed solution sets with measurements from QuEra’s Aquila analog quantum device.
Apply classical Houdayer cluster updates to expand the sampled solution sets.
Measure diversity amplification and manifold coverage using known exact ground-state degeneracies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 43 instances, median diversity amplification was 24.3× and median ground-state manifold recovery was 21%, with complete recovery for six instances and improved solution quality in some cases.
infographic.watch_item: The method is non-ergodic, so it cannot guarantee complete ground-state manifold coverage.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
